description: A multidisciplinary symposium bringing together researchers, clinicians, educators, pharmacologists, trainees, and experts across maternal and child health, precision medicine, translational science, and implementation science to advance safe, effective, and individualized pharmacotherapy for pregnant women, fetuses, and children. The symposium will provide a forum to explore emerging science, identify critical evidence gaps, and foster interdisciplinary collaborations to improve pharmacotherapy for maternal and pediatric populations. Join us for two days of multidisciplinary discussions on advancing safer, more effective, and individualized pharmacotherapy for pregnant women, fetuses, and children. description: The original Gratitude in Action Webinar was first developed and introduced to the UC community in November 2023 as a part of the FSAP Wellness Webinar Series. We invite you now to join us for what has become our Annual November Gratitude Webinar for another opportunity to engage, re-engage, and learn more about developing your own personal practice of Mindful Gratitude. This webinar explores current research on gratitude, including its potential benefits for managing stress, our own wellbeing, and how we experience and respond to the world around us. Given the unique experiences and demands of the UC Community in mind, this webinar will focus on brief, practical approaches to gratitude that can be incorporated into everyday life. Whether you’re interested in returning to a gratitude practice you’ve used before, have tried gratitude practices in the past that didn’t quite work for you, or are simply curious about where to begin, this webinar will help you explore different approaches and identify what might be most useful and sustainable for you. As we head into the winter season, join us for an hour of your workday to step away from the usual demands, learn what the research tells us about gratitude, and experiment with a few ways of putting it into practice. During this webinar, participants will: • Learn about current research on gratitude and its potential benefits for well-being • Explore different approaches to incorporating gratitude into daily life • Identify common barriers to starting and maintaining a gratitude practice • Consider how technology, relationships, and the workplace can help support a practice • Experiment with several brief gratitude practices • Develop a personalized plan for incorporating gratitude in a way that feels realistic and sustainable Presenter Bio: Jessica Allanson, PhD, MA, is a licensed clinical psychologist with the Faculty and Staff Assistance Program at UCSF and runs the FSAP Post-Doctoral Fellowship Program. Dr. Allanson has chosen to specialize in recovery from substance use and workplace burnout, working primarily with those in high-intensity work settings and with high-achieving populations. She incorporates empirically-validated skill-based learning as well as industrial/organizational psychology strategies into her work with individual clients, teams, leaders, and learners. Dr. Allanson believes in the power of compassionate education and hopes to use her passion for sharing and teaching to support and empower those who are curious.

description: This event is in-person only, but open to all. To receive the calendar invite, email Julia Wu (Julia.Wu@ucsf.edu) Contemporary mindfulness programs have demonstrated benefits for health and well-being, yet their application within Indigenous communities requires attention to cultural context, historical trauma, and Indigenous ways of knowing. This presentation introduces IndigenousMIND, a community-engaged framework that integrates evidence-based mindfulness approaches with Indigenous cultural practices, including storytelling, ceremony, traditional arts, and relationships with land and community. Drawing on research and collaborations with Indigenous Nations, Dr. Proulx will discuss lessons learned in adapting mindfulness interventions, emerging findings related to stress and cardiovascular health, and opportunities for culturally grounded approaches to integrative health and healing. Jeffrey Proulx, PhD, is a Haudenosaunee (Six Nations) scholar, researcher, and educator whose work focuses on culturally grounded mindfulness interventions andhealth equity in underserved communities. He is adjunct faculty at Brown University, where he has held appointments in Psychiatry and Human Behavior, Behavioral and Social Sciences, and Contemplative Studies. He is also Vice President and co-founder of the Indigenous Mindfulness Coalition, an Indigenous-led nonprofit dedicated to supporting Indigenous well-being through contemplative practices, cultural revitalization, research, and community engagement. Dr. Proulx developed the IndigenousMIND framework, which brings together contemporary mindfulness approaches with Indigenous cultural practices, values, and ways of knowing. His research, supported by the National Institutes of Health and private foundations, explores the potential of culturally adapted mindfulness interventions to address stress, hypertension, intergenerational trauma, and other health disparities. He is also co-editor of Beyond White Mindfulness: Critical Perspectives on Racism, Well-Being, and Liberation (Routledge, 2022). The Osher Center for Integrative Health hosts monthly research seminars that are open to the research and clinical community at large. Seminars are held from September to June and are generally virtual. Presentations cover a wide range of topics relating to integrative health, many with a focus on integrative health equity. Research Seminars are organized by Ariana Thompson-Lastad, PhD and Joanne Qina’au, PhD, MA, E-YT750. Please contact Julia Wu (julia.wu@ucsf.edu) with any questions., powered by Localist, the Community Event Platform

description: Making Health Promotion Meaningful: Community-engaged Strategies for Reaching Diverse Priority Populations Presented by Simona C. Kwon, DrPH, MPH Simona C. Kwon, DrPH, MPH, is an associate professor in the Department of Population Health at NYU Grossman School of Medicine and serves as director of the NYU Center for the Study of Asian American Health. She is nationally recognized for her expertise in community-based participatory research (CBPR) and health equity initiatives aimed at reducing health disparities in immigrant and minority populations. Dr. Kwon’s research focuses on chronic disease prevention, cultural competency in healthcare, and the social determinants of health. She has led multiple NIH-funded projects addressing health issues in underserved communities, with a particular focus on Asian American populations. As a leader in public health, Dr. Kwon collaborates with community-based organizations to design and implement culturally tailored interventions. Her work highlights the importance of building trust and partnerships between healthcare systems and the communities they serve. She has published extensively on CBPR methodologies and health equity frameworks. Dr. Kwon is committed to advancing inclusive and equitable approaches to improving health outcomes across diverse populations. Learning Objectives: At the end of this activity, learners will be able to: Apply key principles of social marketing and cultural adaptation that can inform efforts to close gaps between current and ideal practice in health promotion and disease prevention for reaching priority populations. Describe how community engagement, participatory approaches, and cultural relevance can support more whole-person, integrated care through clinical practice, research, and education for diverse priority populations. Identify broad strategies for adapting evidence-based health programs to improve relevance, implementation, and sustainability in priority communities, with the goal of improving health outcomes. description: The UCSF Helen Diller Family Comprehensive Cancer Center's Office of Community Engagement presents: CAB2: Chat & Chew Lecture Series Speaker: Mark Jesus Mendoza Magbanua, MS, PhD Laboratory Medicine Helen Diller Family Comprehensive Cancer Center UC San Francisco Talk Title: Can a Blood Test Help Us Stay One Step Ahead of Breast Cancer? Understanding Liquid Biopsy and Its Potential to Improve Cancer Care About the Speaker: Dr. Magbanua is a Professional Researcher/Senior Scientist in the Department of Laboratory Medicine at the University of California, San Francisco (UCSF). He has extensive expertise in liquid biopsy, cancer genomics, and data science, with a particular focus on advancing precision oncology in breast cancer. He leads research projects investigating circulating tumor DNA (ctNA) in the I-SPY trial, an adaptive clinical trial evaluating neoadjuvant therapies for earty-stage breast cancer. His earlier research focused on developing technologies to detect and characterize circulating tumor cells (CTs), contributing to advances in liquid biopsy research. His work has provided important insights into the clinical significance and biological characteristics of tDNA and CTCs in breast cancer. As a principal investigator of NCI-funded R01 research grants, Dr. Magbanua focuses on integrating tDNA with imaging, molecular, and clinical biomarkers to improve the prediction of treatment response and ong-term outcomes in early-stage breast cancer. His research also explores innovative approaches for solating and characterizing tumor cells and analyzing cell-free DNA in malignant effusions from patients with metastatic breast cancer. His overarching goal is to develop and clinically validate liquid biopsy technologies that enable more precise treatment decisions and ultimately improve outcomes for cancer patients., powered by Localist, the Community Event Platform
